answer.label: Not Confucius — a modern saying, coiner unknown
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · modern — best known from a 2015 French novel
answer.sourceLine: The test for a Confucius quotation is the Analects, and this fails it. There is no passage in any of the twenty books that says this, and — the point that settles it — there is no Chinese original for it to be a translation of. Genuine Confucius lines can be checked character by character; this one has nothing underneath it. The most prominent place it appears is as the title of Raphaëlle Giordano’s 2015 French novel, Ta deuxième vie commence quand tu comprends que tu n’en as qu’une, a huge bestseller published in English as Your Second Life Begins When You Realize You Only Have One. We could not establish who said it first.

source.excerpt: The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'
trail: Confucius is easier to check than most misquoted figures, because the corpus is small, fixed and bilingual. The Analects runs to twenty books, and every English rendering sits over a known Chinese text. A genuine saying can be traced to a specific chapter and its characters. This one cannot be traced to any chapter, and no Chinese wording of it exists — which is the giveaway, since a translation without an original is not a translation.

The prominent modern appearance is French. Raphaëlle Giordano’s novel Ta deuxième vie commence quand tu comprends que tu n’en as qu’une was published in 2015 and became one of the decade’s biggest French sellers; the English edition carries the sentence as its title the editions ↗.

What we could not establish is who coined it, or whether the Confucius label was already attached before the novel appeared. Two other names circulate — the actor Tom Hiddleston and the Brazilian modernist Mário de Andrade — and neither has a verifiable first source either. We are recording the gap rather than picking a winner.
source.excerptNote: This is what Confucius actually says about time running out, in James Legge’s Victorian translation of Analects 9.17 — 逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜. Standing by a river, he says only that it goes, and does not stop. No second life, no turning point, no instruction. The modern saying takes the same anxiety and converts it into a self-improvement prompt, which is exactly the thing Confucius does not do here.

source.rightsNote: The excerpt is safe: the Analects is ancient and James Legge’s translation dates from the nineteenth century, so both the Chinese and this English rendering are public domain. The saying at the top of this page is not covered by that. It has no identified author and no established first publication, so its status cannot be determined — and Raphaëlle Giordano’s 2015 novel and its English translation are firmly in copyright, as is any title-page use of the sentence. Attribute it as anonymous and modern; do not attribute it to Confucius. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher & teacher, subject of the Analects
author.bio: Confucius — Kong Fuzi — taught in fifth-century BC China, and what survives of him is the Analects, a compact record of his conversations assembled by his students after his death. In English he functions less as a historical thinker than as a brand for compressed wisdom, which is why he collects modern aphorisms the way Einstein collects modern science jokes. The irony is that he is one of the easiest figures to check: the corpus is short, numbered by book and chapter, and available in the original Chinese, so anyone can confirm in a minute that a given line is not there.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Confucius is the most convenient name in English for a saying that wants to sound old and calm. This one is neither, and unlike most fakes it has a very clear negative test available.

items.why: It is in none of the twenty books of the Analects, and no Chinese wording of it exists. That second point is decisive: every real Confucius quotation in English is a translation of specific characters, and there are no characters here.

Her novel takes the sentence for its title and sold in enormous numbers in France, which is how most European readers met it. We cannot show that she invented it, and we are not going to claim she did the editions ↗.

A slightly different wording — ‘we all have two lives; the second one starts when we realize we only have one’ — circulates under the actor’s name. No interview, script or dated statement has ever been produced for it.
The Brazilian modernist’s name is attached through a widely shared poem about ageing that is itself of doubtful authorship. Two shaky attributions do not make one solid one.
No first printing, in any language, that we can stand behind. We would rather leave that visible than invent an Analects chapter number to fill the space.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous modern saying with no Chinese original and no identified author. It is not in the Analects, and its best-known home is the title of a French novel published in 2015.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It offers a second chance without asking anything in return: the turning point is a realisation, not an action, so you can have your new life simply by reading the sentence and agreeing with it. That is a very efficient piece of comfort, and it explains the sharing numbers.

The Confucius label converts it from an opinion into an inheritance. Attributing it to a man who died in 479 BC implies that people have always known this, which makes it feel less like advice and more like a law of nature.
context.detailsSummary: What Confucius really says about running out of time
detailsBody: Analects 9.17: standing by a river, the Master remarks that it passes on and does not stop, day or night.
That is the whole passage. It is an observation, not a programme — no second life, no threshold, no instruction to seize the day.
The Confucian answer to mortality is elsewhere and is far less comfortable: cultivate character, fulfil your obligations, and keep learning, on the grounds that this is simply what a person is for.
You can check all of this yourself in a few minutes. The Analects is short, numbered by book and chapter, and freely available in Chinese and in Legge’s public-domain English.
That accessibility is exactly why an unlocatable ‘Confucius’ line should make you suspicious.
context.pull: A translation with no original underneath it is not a translation.
